blocks.raw: <Tip>When evaluating EPD data, note the system boundary: A1-A3 (cradle-to-gate) enables material comparison but excludes transport and installation. Full A1-C4 lifecycle assessments are more comprehensive but vary based on assumed service lives and end-of-life scenarios. Always confirm which modules are included in the EPD you are using. For timber, always consider sequestration credit (Module D): timber's negative embodied carbon (stored carbon) is a significant advantage over mineral materials when carbon accounting includes sequestration.</Tip>

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeCard title="Confusing Embodied Carbon with Operational Carbon" severity="critical">Candidates often treat embodied carbon (A1-A3, product production) as equivleant to operational carbon (B6-B7, energy consumption). Operational carbon is typically 3-5 times larger than embodied carbon over a 50-year building life. For decarbonization strategy, focusing on operational efficiency (HVAC, envelope, renewable energy) has immediate large impact, while embodied carbon reduction affects only 15-30 percent of total emissions.</WikiMistakeCard>

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeCard title="Assuming All Timber Carbon is Stored Carbon" severity="critical">Candidates sometimes claim that all timber has negative embodied carbon without accounting for forest sustainability and regrowth. Carbon sequestration is only climate-beneficial if the forest is replanted and regrows after harvest. Deforestation (permanent forest conversion to other use) means carbon storage is temporary; the forest does not regrow to re-sequester the carbon. Candidates must verify FSC or PEFC certification to ensure sustainable harvest before claiming carbon credit.</WikiMistakeCard>

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeCard title="Overestimating Module D (Recycling Credits)" severity="high">Module D assigns credits for future reuse and recycling potential, but actual recycling depends on market demand and facility availability. Candidates sometimes use overly optimistic Module D credits without verifying that recycling infrastructure exists. In the Philippines, recycling rates are low (less than 5% for C&D waste); assuming all segregated material will be recycled may overstate lifecycle carbon credits by 10-30 percent.</WikiMistakeCard>

blocks.raw:
• Assuming A1-A3 embodied carbon values are identical for all producers of a material; actual values vary by location, energy source (renewable vs coal-powered production), and process efficiency
  • Forgetting to account for transport distance (A4) in embodied carbon; importing materials increases A4 emissions significantly versus locally sourced materials
  • Confusing service life with building design life; replacing components (B4 module) during occupancy adds embodied carbon not accounted for in A1-C4 baseline LCA
  • Using single-year operational carbon (B6-B7) without accounting for climate variation, occupancy changes, or future energy grid decarbonization over 50-year building life
  • Applying international EPD data without adjusting for Philippine electricity grid composition (40-45% coal) and transport distances from manufacturing hubs to remote regions
  • Assuming Module D (recycling credits) equal 100% of material value; recycling efficiency losses and contamination typically reduce Module D credits to 30-80% of theoretical potential
